newsitem.title: lesotho: Lesotho army attacks rebel police, 33 surrender.
newsitem.headline: Lesotho army attacks rebel police, 33 surrender.

text.p: At least 33 rebel policemen -- including their leader -- surrendered to Lesotho's army on Sunday under a sustained onslaught to flush out the mutinous officers occupying police headquarters, a diplomat said.
"We have 33 people who have given themselves up including Modise, who is the leader of the rebels," a Western diplomat in Lesotho's capital Maseru told Reuters.

"There are still some policemen in the headquarters. They (the army) intend using teargas and storming the building within the next 40 minutes to an hour if they don't surrender," he said, speaking at 9.35 a.m. (0735 GMT).
Heavy gunfire erupted in the southern African kingdom's capital early on Sunday as army troops loyal to Prime Minister Ntsu Mokhehle's government moved in to subdue an 11-day-old mutiny by policemen.

A Reuters correspondent on the scene said heavy-calibre machineguns, automatic rifles and hand grenades were being used. Intermittent gunfire continued to echo around the capital some three hours after shooting started with a heavy 15-minute barrage at 6.30 a.m. (0430 GMT).
The mutiny began when eight officers seized control of the police headquarters in Lesotho, which is surrounded by and reliant on the region's economic giant South Africa.

Up to 60 other policemen were reported to have joined them in occupying the police headquarters since their siege began and the mutiny has led to a national police strike since the rebels called on officers to support their cause on Thursday.
South Africa on Saturday threw its weight behinf the Lesotho government and said it should quell the mutiny.
In Maseru, two armoured cars speeded around the police headquarters firing at the building with mounted machineguns amidst bursts of shouts over a loudhailer to the rebels: "Come out, come out."
After the partial surrender, army troops began calling the rebel policemen by name.
A crowd of 20 people gathered about 200 metres (yards) from an army roadblock at the police headquarters said they saw 11 people come out of the building, hands up in surrender.

"We see this action (the mutiny) as more symbolic than as real resistance. The police were not trained for war and they are very few in number compared to the army," said an engineer who asked not to be named. "People want to know what is really going on here but the government is reluctant to address us."
Soldiers from the Lesotho Defence Force were guarding the main entrance to the capital and were blocking traffic from entering the city centre.
The eight mutinous officers were resisting arrest for the alleged killing of three fellow officers in 1995.
They demanded amnesty under Lesotho's Pardons Act, which stipulates that security force members may not be charged for any crimes committed from 1993 to 1995.
